2027-07-06.title: Tuesday of the Fourteenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: You have striven with God and with humans, and have prevailed
I shall behold your face in righteousness
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few
2027-07-06.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 14 (Year I). Optional memorial of St Maria Goretti, virgin and martyr (red or white). Verse numbering of Genesis 32 and Psalm 17 is given in NRSV numbering; the Lectionary numbers differ slightly. Liturgical colour: green (red for the memorial).
2027-07-06.verse: When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
theo: Twenty years have passed since Jacob ran away from Esau, and now he is coming home. News has reached him that his brother is coming to meet him with four hundred men. Jacob has done what a man can do: he has prayed (Genesis 32:9–12), sent gifts ahead in droves, divided his camp, and sent his wives and children across the ford of the Jabbok. And then: “Jacob was left alone; and a man wrestled with him until daybreak.” The Bible does not explain who the stranger is. When the man cannot win, he strikes Jacob's hip and puts it out of joint. And Jacob, in pain, holds on: “I will not let you go, unless you bless me.” This is the wrestler's prayer. Then comes the question of the name: “What is your name?” “Jacob.” In Hebrew the name means “heel-grabber,” and at his birth it recalled how he clung to Esau's heel. The man gives him a new name: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with humans, and have prevailed.” Jacob asks for the stranger's name and receives only a blessing; and he calls the place Peniel, “face of God”: “I have seen God face to face, and yet my life is preserved.” “The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, limping because of his hip.” The prophet Hosea remembers the story and adds a detail that Genesis does not give: “He strove with the angel and prevailed, he wept and sought his favor.” Prayer, says the Catechism, can be a struggle in the night, in which we do not let go until God blesses us (Catechism 2573). The one who wrestled and was wounded walks away with a blessing and a limp: he who grabbed at the heel is now the father of the people of Israel. And the Israelites to this day do not eat the thigh muscle, in remembrance. We honour the Jewish people who bear that name. The psalm adds the prayer of a man who has come through the night and looks forward to the morning: “As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake I shall be satisfied, beholding your likeness.”

Matthew is gathering the Lord's mighty works, and this is the last of the series. A man who is mute and possessed is brought to Jesus; the demon is driven out; “the one who had been mute spoke.” The crowds are astonished: “Never has anything like this been seen in Israel.” But some of the Pharisees say, “By the ruler of the demons he casts out the demons.” This is the first sign of the opposition that will grow in the Gospel, and it is a warning that a heart may see a miracle and still close itself. Then Matthew gives a summary of the Lord's work: Jesus “went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and curing every disease and every sickness.” And a sentence follows that shows his heart: “When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.” The Greek verb for compassion means to be moved in one's innermost being, in the gut. The crowds are people who have been worn down by hunger, taxes, illness and false leaders, and Jesus feels it. He takes up the promise of the prophet Ezekiel: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep ... I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak.” And then he turns to his disciples: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.” The first thing he asks is that we pray, and in the next chapter the Twelve will be sent. Many people in India, and in Kerala especially, know what a harvest is, and know that the rains are only the start. The harvest of souls is also great today, and it needs workers, priests, religious, catechists and lay people. St Maria Goretti, whom the Church remembers today, was a field that bore a harvest at a very early age. Born in 1890 in a poor farming family in Italy, she was an eleven-year-old girl when, on 5 July 1902, a young man living in the same house, Alessandro Serenelli, tried to force her into sin. She refused: “No, it is a sin. God does not want it.” He stabbed her repeatedly, and she died the next day in the hospital at Nettuno, forgiving him. Alessandro was sentenced to thirty years in prison; some years later he dreamed that Maria offered him lilies, and he changed. Released in 1929, he asked her mother Assunta for forgiveness, and was present at Maria's canonisation in 1950. He died in 1970, as a lay brother of the Capuchins. Her life shows both the cost of purity and the power of forgiveness.
outline: Ask: when did you last wrestle with God in prayer, and refuse to let go?
Point 1 · I will not let you go
Jacob at the Jabbok: a night of struggle, a new name, a blessing and a limp.
Jesus sees harassed and helpless people as sheep without a shepherd, and his heart moves.
Point 3 · The harvest and the labourers
Pray to the Lord of the harvest; vocations begin on our knees.
A girl of eleven who said no to sin, and yes to forgiveness.
“I will not let you go, unless you bless me.”
live: Choose one real need and pray for it for ten minutes each day this week without giving up, as Jacob did: I will not let you go unless you bless me.
Each day this week say one Hail Mary for priests, sisters and brothers, and for young people who may be called. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send labourers.
saints: Born at Corinaldo in Italy to a poor farming family; after her father Luigi died of malaria, she took on much of the household work with her mother Assunta. A girl of deep prayer, she prepared with great care for her First Communion at eleven. On 5 July 1902, at Le Ferriere, she was attacked by a nineteen-year-old neighbour, Alessandro Serenelli, who tried to force her into sin. She resisted and was stabbed fourteen times. She died the next day in hospital, having forgiven him. He later repented, and he attended her canonisation by Pope Pius XII in 1950. She is a patroness of youth, and of those who have been victims of violence.
2027-07-06.prayer: God of Jacob, who wrestled with your servant in the night and blessed him with a new name, teach us to hold on to you in prayer, even when it costs us, and to walk in the morning of your blessing. Lord Jesus, shepherd of the harassed and helpless, move our hearts with your compassion, and send labourers into your harvest. Through the intercession of St Maria Goretti, who kept her purity and forgave her murderer, give our young people a love for what is pure and a heart ready to forgive. Amen.
altar: At Mass we hold on to the Lord with Jacob's persistence: we do not let you go, unless you bless us. And he blesses us, not with a new name but with himself. The compassion that moved Jesus when he saw the crowds is present in the Eucharist, where the Good Shepherd feeds his sheep with his own Body. Before Communion we pray for the grace of forgiveness, as we say: forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us. St Maria Goretti received Holy Communion for the first time a few weeks before her death, and the bread of the strong made her ready to forgive.

quick: Jacob wrestles with a stranger at the Jabbok until daybreak, receives the name Israel, a blessing and a limp.
Jacob names the place Peniel: he has seen God face to face and lives.
Jesus heals a mute man, has compassion on the crowds like sheep without a shepherd, and asks his disciples to pray for labourers for the harvest.
2027-07-06.action: Pray ten minutes today without giving up, and say one Hail Mary for vocations.
2027-07-06.question: Do I hold on to the Lord in prayer until he blesses me, or do I give up when he does not answer quickly?
kidsaint: Maria lived in a small house in Italy. Her family was poor, her father died, and Maria helped her mother with cooking, cleaning and caring for the little ones. She loved Jesus very much and prayed every day. She made her First Communion when she was eleven. One day a young man who lived nearby tried to make her do something bad. Maria said: no, it is a sin! God does not want it! The young man hurt her badly, and she died the next day. Before she died, she said she forgave him. Years later he said sorry and became a good man. Lesson: say no to sin, and forgive those who hurt you.

family.explain: Jacob was alone by a river at night when a stranger wrestled with him until morning. Jacob would not let go. He said: bless me! And the stranger gave him a new name, Israel, and blessed him. Jacob said: I have seen God face to face! In the Gospel, Jesus looked at big crowds and felt sorry for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. He said: the harvest is big, but there are few workers. Let us pray that God sends more workers!
family.intention: We pray for priests, sisters, brothers and teachers of the faith, and for children who may be called to serve God.
family.ask: Ask: “What would it mean for us to ask God again and again for something, without giving up?”

illus: A woman of a coastal parish near Kollam had prayed for twelve years for her husband, who had stopped going to church after a loss in business. Each evening she prayed the rosary at the foot of a small crucifix, saying to the Lord quietly: I will not let you go until you bless him. Her friends told her to stop; the husband laughed at her. But one morning he came down to the kitchen and said: take me to Mass. He never said what had changed. Only that he had heard her through the wall the night before, speaking to the Lord as if wrestling with him, and that he did not want her to wrestle alone. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: God of Jacob, we do not let go of you. Lord of the harvest, send labourers into your harvest. Amen.
share: I will not let you go, unless you bless me (Genesis 32:26). What blessing am I asking for, and how long have I been asking?
He had compassion for them (Matthew 9:36). Whom do I see as harassed and helpless?
Ask the Lord of the harvest (Matthew 9:38). How could I help a young person to listen to God's call?
pm.resp: I shall behold your face in righteousness.
interc: For those who struggle in prayer, that they may not give up.
For vocations to the priesthood, the religious life and lay missions.
For young people, that they may follow St Maria Goretti's love of purity.
For victims of violence, and for the grace of forgiveness for those who have been hurt.
For our group, that we may hold on to the Lord in faith.
pm.close: Father, you gave Jacob the name Israel after a night of struggle. Give us perseverance in prayer and zeal for your harvest. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, have you ever prayed all night? Not just words, but a real struggle? Jacob did. He is returning home after twenty years, and his brother Esau is coming with four hundred men. Jacob has prayed, sent gifts, arranged his camp. And now, alone at the river in the dark, a man wrestles with him until morning (Genesis 32:25). We do not know exactly who he is. But in the end Jacob says: I have seen God face to face.

Why does God wrestle with Jacob? Because Jacob has to be changed. All his life, he has gripped, grabbed and bargained. That is the meaning of his name: heel-grabber. Now he is gripping God. And God lets him, because this struggle is a prayer. The man touches his hip, and Jacob will limp for the rest of his life. And still he says: I will not let you go, unless you bless me (Genesis 32:26). And God blesses him and gives him a new name: Israel. He walks away limping, but he walks away blessed.

Dear friends, are there nights in your life like that? A sick child, a failing business, a broken marriage, a doubt that will not leave? Do not be afraid to wrestle with God. He can take it. And he does not mind if we say, I will not let you go. In the morning we may be limping, but we will have a blessing, and we will have seen his face.

In the Gospel Jesus walks through the towns and villages, and he sees the crowds. And Matthew says he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). What does Jesus do with that compassion? He turns to his disciples and says: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest (Matthew 9:37–38). Notice, he does not say: go! He says: pray! The first step is prayer. Let us pray today, for priests, religious sisters, brothers, catechists and for our own children, that they may hear the call.

Today the Church remembers St Maria Goretti. She was eleven. She was attacked by a young man in her own home, and she said no, because she knew that it was a sin. She died the next day, forgiving him. And that forgiveness bore fruit: Alessandro repented, and years later he knelt beside her mother, asking pardon. That is a harvest. A girl of eleven, a poor farm child, was a labourer in the Lord's harvest. May all our young people have her courage and her forgiving heart.
kids: Children, Jacob was alone by a river in the night, and a stranger wrestled with him until morning. Jacob would not let go! He said: bless me! And God blessed him and gave him a new name, Israel. Jacob walked away with a limp, but happy, because he had seen God. When we pray for something, we can keep on praying, like Jacob. Today we remember St Maria Goretti. She was only eleven. When someone wanted her to do something bad, she said: no, God does not want it! And before she died, she forgave the man who hurt her. Let us say no to sin, and let us forgive.

intro: Theme: “I will not let you go, unless you bless me.”
Jacob's night at the Jabbok, the compassion of the Shepherd for the harassed crowd, and the harvest that begins on our knees.

points.h: I will not let you go
sub: Alone at the ford in the night.
A new name and a limp.
I have seen God face to face.
q: Then he said, “Let me go, for the day is breaking.” But Jacob said, “I will not let you go, unless you bless me.”
Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart.
points.apply: Pray for one real need for ten minutes a day this week, without giving up.

sub: A girl of eleven who forgave.
q: Those who go out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, carrying their sheaves.
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
points.apply: Say a Hail Mary every day this week for vocations, and ask St Maria Goretti to help the young.

concl: Jacob wrestles all night, refuses to let go until God blesses him, and is given the name Israel, a blessing and a limp.
Jesus has compassion on the harassed crowd, asks us to pray for labourers, and finds a harvest even in an eleven-year-old girl who said no to sin and forgave her killer.
